questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish performance from scalability?
options: They are the same quality attribute described with two different words

Scalability is how a design holds up as volume and concurrency grow over time; performance is how fast a specific page or transaction completes right now -- a design can be strong on one and weak on the other
Performance only matters for Experience Cloud sites
Scalability is a developer's concern, while performance is purely an admin's concern
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the two: a design can be scalable for future volume but slow today, or fast today but headed for scalability trouble -- they need separate evaluation.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by 'perceived performance' diverging from measured performance?
options: Perceived performance is just a marketing term with no real basis
A page that shows meaningful content quickly (even if full load takes longer) can feel faster to a user than a page that measures faster overall but shows nothing until everything is ready
Perceived performance only applies to mobile devices
Measured performance is always identical to perceived performance by definition
questions.explain: The lesson gives the example of a four-second page that shows key content within half a second often feeling faster than a three-second page that shows nothing until fully loaded -- load order and what appears first matters architecturally.

questions.q: Why does this lesson flag a Lightning record page with a dozen components, each independently querying its own data, as a performance risk?
options: Because Lightning pages are limited to a maximum of five components
Because each independent query multiplies round-trips, in a way a well-designed aggregate query or a more deliberate component selection would avoid
Because components cannot query data at all without an Apex controller
Because this is actually a scalability-only concern, never a performance one
questions.explain: Many components each independently fetching their own data multiplies network/query round-trips, which is a common, avoidable performance cause this lesson names directly.

questions.q: Per this lesson, how can synchronous automation turn an architecture choice into user-perceived lag?
options: Synchronous automation never affects what the user experiences

Automation that performs a slow external callout or heavy calculation synchronously, blocking the save, creates lag the user directly feels -- when that work could instead run asynchronously after the save completes
Synchronous automation always runs faster than asynchronous automation in every case
This only applies to Batch Apex, never to triggers or Flow
questions.explain: Doing slow work synchronously in the critical path of a save blocks the user directly; deferring that same work to run asynchronously after the save removes it from what the user has to wait on.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue performance should be a design-time responsibility rather than a post-launch fix?
options: Because performance problems discovered after launch via user complaints are often far more expensive to fix, since the fix may require restructuring a page or data model real users and data already depend on
Because performance problems never occur if a page uses standard Salesforce components
Because Salesforce automatically re-architects slow pages without developer involvement
Because performance only matters during the first month after go-live
questions.explain: The lesson's core practical argument is that catching a performance issue during design review is cheaper than fixing it after real users and data already depend on the existing structure.
